paragraphs.title: The Fool's Fate and the Human Tendency to Sin

easy.explanation: Eliphaz says, “I would seek unto God, and unto God would I commit my cause.”
easy.q: Whom does Eliphaz say a person should seek?

easy.explanation: Job 5:2 says, “For wrath killeth the foolish man.”
easy.q: What happens to the foolish man according to Eliphaz?

easy.explanation: The children are described as being “far from safety” with no one to deliver them.
easy.q: What happens to the fool's children?

medium.explanation: The hungry eat his harvest and take it even out of the thorns.
medium.q: Why is the fool's harvest taken away?

answers: Whom a person will seek for help
Which field a person will cultivate
Where a person will build a house
medium.explanation: Eliphaz asks whom a person will turn to, contrasting human help with seeking God.
medium.q: In the question, “to which of the saints wilt thou turn,” what is Eliphaz asking?

answers: Trouble does not come from the dust, and man is born to trouble
medium.explanation: The passage says affliction does not come from the dust, yet man is born unto trouble.
medium.q: What conclusion does Eliphaz make in verses 6–7?

answers: Wrath and envy lead to destruction
challenge.explanation: Wrath kills the foolish man, and envy slays the silly one.
challenge.q: What connection does Eliphaz make between the fool's emotions and his fate?

answers: Trouble is connected to a broader human condition
People are unaffected by their actions
challenge.explanation: The final verse broadens the thought by saying that man is born unto trouble.
challenge.q: What is suggested by the movement from the fool's situation to humanity in general?

challenge.explanation: The passage mentions his habitation, children, harvest, and substance.
challenge.q: Which detail shows that the fool's troubles affect more than the fool himself?

paragraphs.title: God's Greatness and the Reversal of Fortunes

easy.explanation: He says, “I would seek unto God, and unto God would I commit my cause.”
easy.q: To whom does Eliphaz say he would commit his cause?

easy.explanation: God gives rain upon the earth and sends waters upon the fields.
easy.q: What does God send upon the earth?

answers: Those that mourn and are lowly
easy.explanation: God sets up those that are low and exalts those that mourn to safety.
easy.q: Whom does God exalt to safety?

medium.explanation: God does great things and unsearchable, marvelous things without number.
medium.q: How is God's greatness described in verse 9?

medium.explanation: The crafty are those who devise plans that God disappoints.
medium.q: What does the word “crafty” describe in this passage?

medium.explanation: The text says, “He disappointeth the devices of the crafty.”
medium.q: What does God do to the devices of the crafty?

answers: The lowly are exalted while the crafty fail
challenge.explanation: God raises the lowly and saves the poor while frustrating the plans of the crafty.
challenge.q: How are fortunes reversed in this passage?

answers: Both show God's life-giving and helpful power
The rain is presented as punishment
challenge.explanation: Rain shows God's provision, while deliverance shows His care for the needy.
challenge.q: What relationship exists between the rain and God's deliverance?

answers: Their hands cannot perform their enterprise
challenge.explanation: God disappoints their devices so that their hands cannot carry out their plans.
challenge.q: Which detail emphasizes the helplessness of the crafty?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “Behold, happy is the man whom God correcteth.”
Eliphaz says, “Therefore despise not thou the chastening of the Almighty.”
easy.q: What should a person not despise?

answers: He binds up and makes whole
easy.explanation: God wounds, but His hands also bind up and make whole.
easy.q: What does God do after wounding?

answers: As discipline that should not be despised
medium.explanation: Eliphaz connects suffering with the chastening of the Almighty.
medium.q: How are suffering and correction presented in Eliphaz's words?

medium.explanation: Chastening refers to corrective discipline intended to instruct.
medium.q: What does “chastening” mean in this context?

medium.explanation: God makes sore and binds up; He wounds and makes whole.
medium.q: Which pair of actions describes God's treatment of the person?

answers: Suffering may be part of a process of correction and restoration
challenge.explanation: The contrast presents God's discipline together with His power to restore.
challenge.q: What does the contrast between wounding and healing suggest about suffering?

answers: Because God's chastening should not be despised
Because suffering has no connection to God
challenge.explanation: Eliphaz tells the listener not to despise the Almighty's chastening.
challenge.q: Why does Eliphaz call for a changed attitude toward suffering?

answers: He maketh sore, and bindeth up; He woundeth, and his hands make whole
challenge.explanation: The paired expressions place injury beside healing.
challenge.q: Which parallel wording strengthens the idea of God's double action?

paragraphs.title: Deliverance from Every Trouble and Divine Protection

easy.explanation: The verse says, “He shall deliver thee in six troubles: yea, in seven.”
easy.q: From how many troubles does the passage say God will deliver?

easy.explanation: In famine, God redeems the person from death.
easy.q: From what does God redeem a person in famine?

easy.explanation: The passage says the person shall not be afraid of the beasts of the earth.
easy.q: What should the person not fear?

answers: Famine, war, harmful speech, and robbery
medium.explanation: The passage mentions famine, war, the scourge of the tongue, and destruction.
medium.q: Which dangers are included in God's protection?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes injury caused by malicious or harmful words.
medium.q: What does “the scourge of the tongue” mean?

answers: The natural world is no longer a threat and is part of the person's peace
The person becomes a wild animal
medium.explanation: The stones and beasts of the field are presented as peaceful rather than dangerous.
medium.q: What is meant by being “in league with the stones of the field”?

answers: By listing many different dangers from which God delivers
challenge.explanation: The passage lists troubles, famine, war, harmful speech, destruction, and wild animals.
challenge.q: How is the sense of protection built in verses 19–23?

answers: God's protection extends across many areas of life
challenge.explanation: The passage includes both human dangers and dangers associated with the natural world.
challenge.q: What is suggested by the movement from protection against enemies to protection in nature?

answers: God's protection enables the person to live without fear of these dangers
challenge.explanation: Because God delivers and protects, the person need not be afraid.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between fearlessness and deliverance?

paragraphs.title: Peace at Home and a Good End

easy.explanation: The verse says, “Thou shalt know that thy tabernacle shall be in peace.”
easy.q: What will the person know about his tabernacle?

answers: Great as the grass of the earth
easy.explanation: His seed shall be great, and his offspring as the grass of the earth.
easy.q: How are the person's descendants described?

easy.explanation: He comes to his grave in a full age, like a shock of corn gathered in its season.
easy.q: How does the person's life end according to the passage?

answers: A peaceful tabernacle and a habitation without sin
medium.explanation: The verse describes a peaceful tabernacle and visiting the habitation without sin.
medium.q: What does peace in the household include in verse 24?

answers: After a complete and fulfilled life
medium.explanation: The phrase describes reaching the grave after a full life.
medium.q: What does “in a full age” mean in this context?

answers: Hear and know the teaching for himself
medium.explanation: Eliphaz says, “Hear it, and know thou it for thy good.”
medium.q: What does Eliphaz ask Job to do at the end?

answers: Protection results in peace at home, many descendants, and a good end
Protection is limited to the fields
challenge.explanation: The final verses describe the peaceful results of God's care.
challenge.q: How does the ending connect with the earlier idea of protection?

answers: Death at the proper time after a full life
challenge.explanation: The image presents death as a harvest gathered in its proper season.
challenge.q: What does the image of a shock of corn coming in its season suggest?

answers: It presents Eliphaz's teaching as examined and established
challenge.explanation: Eliphaz concludes that the teaching has been searched out and urges Job to hear it for his good.
challenge.q: What is the function of “Lo this, we have searched it, so it is”?
